explanations.explanation: Micah says the remnant of Jacob will be "like dew from the LORD" in the midst of many peoples (Micah 5:7). Dew just shows up on the grass, quiet and gentle, and nobody has to order it. I think that's a lovely picture to open with, friend. Hold onto it, because the next picture is not so quiet.

Hail is a fun guess, friend, but it'd leave dents in everybody's car. Micah says the remnant will be "like dew from the LORD, like showers on the grass" (Micah 5:7). Dew is soft and it comes from the LORD. No ice, no bruises.

Fire from heaven sounds dramatic, I'll give you that. But Micah's first picture is much softer: "like dew from the LORD, like showers on the grass" (Micah 5:7). Dew is gentle, and it comes from the LORD. The fire-and-roaring picture shows up next verse, and it's a lion instead.

Careful, friend, this one has a sneaky second half. The showers part is true, but Micah says the dew and showers "do not wait for man or linger for mankind" (Micah 5:7). They don't wait for anybody. So the statement is false, because it says they DO wait.

Yes, friend. The text says the dew and showers "do not wait for man or linger for mankind" (Micah 5:7). Nobody holds the rain up with a clipboard. The first half of the card was true, since showers on the grass are in the verse, but the waiting part is the opposite of what Micah says.

explanations.answer: A lion among the forest beasts
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Micah says the remnant will be "like a lion among the beasts of the forest" (Micah 5:8). Same remnant, same crowd of nations, brand new picture. The dew was soft and the lion is NOT.

Sheep and wolves is a famous pairing, friend, but it's not what Micah says. His picture is the other way around: "like a lion among the beasts of the forest" (Micah 5:8). The remnant is the lion here. Nobody's hiding behind the fence.

A lily is pretty, friend, but it isn't in this verse. Micah says the remnant will be "like a lion among the beasts of the forest" (Micah 5:8). No flowers here. This is a roaring picture, not a gardening one.

Not quite, friend. Micah says the lion "tramples and tears as it passes through, with no one to rescue them" (Micah 5:8). So nobody comes to rescue them. It's the other way around from what the card says.

Right, friend. The verse says the lion "tramples and tears as it passes through, with no one to rescue them" (Micah 5:8). No one is there to rescue them. I'd say a young lion among sheep has the whole place to itself.
Yes, friend. The words say, "Your hand will be lifted over your foes, and all your enemies will be cut off" (Micah 5:9). Notice it says ALL of them. Nobody gets left standing in the back row.

I like the hopeful guess, friend, but that isn't what the verse says. It says, "all your enemies will be cut off" (Micah 5:9). The hand is lifted over the foes, and then they're cut off. A peace treaty isn't in the text.
That's a creative guess, friend, but Micah doesn't go there. He says, "all your enemies will be cut off" (Micah 5:9). Nothing about hiring them or handing out aprons. They're simply cut off.

Chariots it is, friend. The LORD says, "I will remove your horses from among you and wreck your chariots" (Micah 5:10). Horses and chariots go together like a mixer and a bowl. He takes out the whole set.

Ships make sense for a big list, friend, but they aren't in this verse. The LORD says, "I will remove your horses from among you and wreck your chariots" (Micah 5:10). The horses pair up with chariots, which are made for pulling. No harbor needed.

Wagons are a good guess, since they also roll behind horses, friend. But the LORD names something else: "I will remove your horses from among you and wreck your chariots" (Micah 5:10). Chariots are the word in the verse. Wagons stay in the barn.

That's right, friend. The LORD says, "I will remove the cities of your land and tear down all your strongholds" (Micah 5:11). Cities and strongholds both go on His list. And remember, this is the same list that began with horses and chariots.

This one's true, friend, so it's easy to talk yourself out of it. The LORD says, "I will remove the cities of your land and tear down all your strongholds" (Micah 5:11). Strongholds are right there next to the cities. Both are on the list.

Yes, friend. The LORD says, "I will cut the sorceries from your hand, and you will have no fortune-tellers" (Micah 5:12). The sorceries go, and so do the fortune-tellers. I'd say that's a job nobody saw coming to be gone.

Tax collectors would make a lot of adults cheer, friend, but they aren't in this verse. The LORD says, "I will cut the sorceries from your hand, and you will have no fortune-tellers" (Micah 5:12). The list here is about sorcery and telling fortunes. Your tax bill is safe from this verse.

Gatekeepers are a fair guess for an ancient list, friend, but Micah doesn't mention them. The LORD says, "I will cut the sorceries from your hand, and you will have no fortune-tellers" (Micah 5:12). The word he uses goes with sorceries. Fortune-tellers are the answer.

explanations.answer: So the people stop bowing to their own handiwork
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The LORD says He'll cut off the carved images and sacred pillars "so that you will no longer bow down to the work of your own hands" (Micah 5:13). Think about it. Somebody makes a thing with their hands and then bows to it. I'd say that's like me stamping a cookie and then saluting it.

explanations.answer: So the land has room for more crops
explanations.explanation: Crops would be a practical reason, friend, but the text never says that. The reason it gives is "so that you will no longer bow down to the work of your own hands" (Micah 5:13). It's about bowing, not about planting. I'd stick with what the verse says.

explanations.answer: So the nations cannot carry them off
explanations.explanation: That's an interesting thought, friend, but Micah doesn't give it as the reason. He says it's "so that you will no longer bow down to the work of your own hands" (Micah 5:13). The point is the bowing. Nothing about thieves.

explanations.answer: The ones that have not obeyed Him
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The LORD says He will take vengeance "upon the nations that have not obeyed Me" (Micah 5:15). The verse names the not obeying as the mark of those nations. Nothing is said there about location or warnings.

explanations.answer: The ones that lie closest to Israel
explanations.explanation: Close neighbors is a natural guess, friend, but the verse doesn't mention distance at all. The LORD says, "upon the nations that have not obeyed Me" (Micah 5:15). What marks them is that they have not obeyed. The map isn't part of it.

explanations.answer: The ones that have never been warned
explanations.explanation: I see the thinking, friend, but the verse goes a different direction. The LORD says, "upon the nations that have not obeyed Me" (Micah 5:15). It names not obeying, and it doesn't say anything about whether they were warned. I'd stay with what the text gives us.
